newsitem.title: USA: U.S. investigators doubt bomb letter authenticity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. investigators doubt bomb letter authenticity.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Thursday they were sceptical about the authenticity of an anonymous letter claiming responsibility for the bombings of an Atlanta abortion clinic and a gay and lesbian nightclub.

The handwritten letter, sent to Reuters, NBC and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, claimed credit on behalf of the Army of God, a shadowy militant Christian group that advocates violence against abortion clinics and their staffs.
The letter writer invited the FBI to confirm details about the makeup of the bombs and pointed out specific differences in the devices used in each attack.

But Bobby Browning, a spokesman for the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF), said forensic experts have called the letter into question because of details that might have been listed but were not.
"The letter has omitted some details that would only be familiar to the bomber. So, there is healthy scepticism about the letter," Browning said.

"That's not to say that we're totally discounting the possibility that the bomber may have actually written the letter. It's just to say we can't really take a position right now until we learn a little bit more," he said.
About a dozen people were injured in the two bombings. A total of five bombs have exploded in Atlanta in the past seven months.

On January 16, a bomb exploded outside the Northside Family Planning Services centre in the suburb of Sandy Springs. No one was hurt in the blast. But a second device, hidden in a corner of the parking lot, injured at least six people, mainly rescue workers and law enforcement agents.

Last Friday, five people were hurt when a bomb exploded in the rear patio section of the crowded Otherside Lounge, a bar frequented mainly by lesbians. A second device found at that site was detonated by a police robot.

U.S. officials said most of the details about bomb components contained in the Army of God letter could have been gleaned from the news. But they stopped short of saying the list of components was in any way incorrect.

"The vast majority, if not all of the details about the bombs, had already been reported in news accounts. So we can't differentiate between whether the person writing the letter could have learned about all the components from news accounts or whether they actually had intimate knowledge about the bombs," said Browning.

The letter was postmarked on Saturday from Atlanta, and federal officials believe it could have been mailed no later than noon -- about 12 hours after local television carried the first accounts of the nightclub bombing.
At midday on Saturday, news accounts about the makeup of the nightclub bomb contained few details other than its use of spike nails as shrapnel.
